meta.title: Onset of Quantum Chaos in Random Field Theories
meta.abstractHtml: We study the quantum Lyapunov exponent in theories with spacetime-independent disorder. We first derive self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions for products of models coupled by disorder at large , generalizing the equations appearing in SYK-like models. We then study families of theories in which the disorder coupling is an exactly marginal deformation, allowing us to follow from weak to strong coupling. We find interesting behaviors, including a discontinuous transition into chaos, mimicking classical KAM theory.

children.title: Abstract
children.body: We study the quantum Lyapunov exponent in theories with spacetime-independent disorder. We first derive self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions for products of models coupled by disorder at large , generalizing the equations appearing in SYK-like models. We then study families of theories in which the disorder coupling is an exactly marginal deformation, allowing us to follow from weak to strong coupling. We find interesting behaviors, including a discontinuous transition into chaos, mimicking classical KAM theory.

Systems with disorder are ubiquitous in nature, and display a wide range of interesting physical phenomena. Disorder can sometimes be modeled by introducing random couplings, and averaging over these random couplings can lead to simplifications which allow for exact computations, at least when the number of degrees of freedom is parametrically large. A notable example is the Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev (SYK) model, in which (nearly) conformal symmetry is restored at low energies Sachdev and Ye (1993); Kitaev (2015); Maldacena and Stanford (2016); Kitaev and Suh (2018), and such averages allow for the computation of the quantum chaos exponent . The latter is defined by the fastest growing exponential mode in the double-commutator for generic operators , over an appropriate time scale, with temperature Larkin and Ovchinnikov (1969).

gist.html: Averaging over random couplings, as in SYK, makes the chaos exponent $\lambda_L$, a double commutator's growth rate, computable.

children.title: The double commutator as a Lyapunov exponent
children.body: Classical chaos is sensitivity to initial conditions: a small change $\delta q(0)$ grows as $e^{\lambda t}$, where $\lambda$ is the Lyapunov exponent. Equivalently the Poisson bracket $\{q(t),p(0)\}=\partial q(t)/\partial q(0)$ grows exponentially. The quantum counterpart replaces the bracket by a commutator $[U(t),W(0)]$; it is squared, so that phases do not cancel, and averaged in a thermal state, giving the double commutator. Expanding the square produces correlators whose operators are not time-ordered, often called out-of-time-order correlators. In a large-$N$ system the double commutator starts at order $1/N$ and grows as $e^{\lambda_Lt}/N$ until it is of order one, after a time of order $\log N/\lambda_L$. Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford proved the bound $\lambda_L\le2\pi/\beta$, which black holes and SYK at strong coupling saturate. The paper asks how this exponent leaves zero as interactions are switched on.

The SYK model consists of free quantum mechanical fermions deformed by a relevant all-to-all spacetime-independent disordered interaction. Generalizations have appeared which consist of copies of other free theories with similar interactions Murugan et al. (2017); Fu et al. (2017); Peng (2018); Bulycheva (2018); Chang et al. (2021); Popov (2020); Gross and Rosenhaus (2017); Lian et al. (2019). In this letter we study quantum chaos in a more general setting by studying copies of a general core model (which can be a quantum field theory or a spin system), deformed by a spacetime-independent all-to-all interaction. In particular, we eventually focus on being a conformal field theory (CFT) in 0+1 or in higher dimensions, and with an exactly marginal disorder interaction. In such a setup we have better control over the space of couplings over which we are averaging, eliminating the complications of the renormalization group (RG) and without having to resort to strong coupling.

gist.html: Generalises SYK to $N$ copies of any core model; exactly marginal disorder avoids RG flow and strong coupling.

children.body: We will first derive self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions of at leading order in for general disordered CFTs. These extend known results for disordered free theories like the SYK model Maldacena and Stanford (2016); Kitaev and Suh (2018)), and for spin systems Bray and Moore (1980). We will also discuss similar results for the double-commutator (defined in (7) below). Although these self-consistency equations are complicated, they are tractable in perturbation theory in and allow us to establish the existence of a kernel structure from which we can extract the chaos exponent , which is the rate of growth of a double commutator. The latter is given by the fastest growing eigenvector (with eigenvalue 1) of a specific integral kernel (see equation (9)), as long as this rate of growth is indeed positive Kitaev (2015); Kitaev (2015); Larkin and Ovchinnikov (1969). We will denote by the putative chaos exponent read from the diagonalization .

gist.html: Large-$N$ equations give a kernel whose eigenvalue-one mode yields a putative exponent $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$.

gist.html: The two possible onsets of chaos as $J$ grows: continuous, or discontinuous when $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ starts negative.

children.body: We will be interested in computing the chaos exponent as a function of , as it is varied from weak to strong coupling. The diagonalization of is a difficult process, which can usually be done only when conformal invariance is restored. Normally, the disorder is a relevant deformation. To compute the chaos one first flow to the IR CFT (which is equivalent to take ) and find the chaos exponent there Murugan et al. (2017). In this work we focus on cases where the averaged interacting theory is conformally invariant for all . This can be done by demanding that the disorder interaction itself be exactly marginal, in which case the theory is conformally invariant for every realization of the couplings, and the space of ’s forms a conformal manifold 1. The disorder average is then simply a non-uniform average over this conformal manifold, with no RG-related complications (for recent discussions of averages over conformal manifolds see Maloney and Witten (2020); Afkhami-Jeddi et al. (2021), and for the marginal case see Berkooz et al. (2017)).

gist.html: Exactly marginal disorder keeps the theory conformal at every $J$, so the average is over a conformal manifold.

children.title: Relevant, marginal and exactly marginal couplings
children.body: A CFT in $d$ spacetime dimensions deformed by $g\int d^dx\,\mathcal O$, with $\mathcal O$ of dimension $\Delta$, gives the coupling $g$ a mass dimension $d-\Delta$. If $\Deltad$ it is irrelevant. If $\Delta=d$ it is classically marginal, but quantum corrections usually generate a beta function at second order, $\beta_g\propto g^2$, set by the operator's three-point function with itself, so it becomes marginally relevant or irrelevant. A coupling whose beta function vanishes to all orders is exactly marginal, and its values form a conformal manifold of CFTs. Exact marginality is rare without supersymmetry. In SYK the random coupling is relevant, so its chaos is computed only at the infrared fixed point; the paper chooses exactly marginal random couplings to avoid the flow.

Surprisingly, we will find models where is negative at weak coupling. This signals a breakdown of the approximations involved in the computation, and so in this case the true chaos exponent simply vanishes, . In other words, we have

(3)

As a result, there are two possible behaviors for the onset of chaos: either the theory undergoes a continuous transition into chaos as in figure 1a or a discontinuous transition as in figure 1b, corresponding to whether is non-negative or negative at small enough respectively.2

gist.html: When $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ is negative at weak coupling there is no chaos, so the onset can be discontinuous.

children.body: The discontinuous transition into chaos is a surprising result, and it is tempting to compare it to similar results in classical chaos, the most famous one being the KAM theorem. In order to sharpen the comparison, we also discuss what a single core CFT should obey in order for the transition into chaos to be discontinuous. Similar works on the onset of quantum chaos include Stanford (2016); de Mello Koch et al. (2019); Chowdhury and Swingle (2017); Steinberg and Swingle (2019); Maldacena and Stanford (2016); Peng (2018), and Lian et al. (2019); Hu and Lian (2021) are especially relevant.

gist.html: The discontinuous onset invites comparison with the KAM theorem; the paper asks what a core CFT must obey for it.

children.title: The KAM theorem and the onset of classical chaos
children.body: An integrable Hamiltonian system with $n$ degrees of freedom has $n$ conserved quantities in involution, and its motion winds around invariant $n$-dimensional tori in phase space, quasi-periodically and without chaos. The Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser (KAM) theorem says what happens when such a system is perturbed by a small, smooth term of strength $\epsilon$: tori whose frequencies are sufficiently irrational survive, slightly deformed, and they fill most of phase space, a fraction tending to one as $\epsilon\to0$. Chaos appears only in thin layers around destroyed resonant tori, and spreads over phase space only at larger perturbations. Chaos therefore does not take over as soon as integrability is broken; the onset of widespread chaos happens at a finite perturbation. The paper's discontinuous transition, with a quantum chaos exponent that stays zero up to a finite disorder strength, is what it compares with this classical result.

We will apply our formalism to two classes of examples where the disorder interaction is exactly marginal. The first class is disordered generalized free fields in d (following Gross and Rosenhaus (2017)) and in d. The second class is the disordered supersymmetric (SUSY) minimal models. In practice, we will only discuss the simplest case of the minimal model here. We will find a discontinuous transition in the former and a continuous transition in the latter.

gist.html: Examples: disordered generalized free fields (a discontinuous onset) and a disordered $\mathcal N=2$ minimal model (a continuous one).

children.body: More details and discussions on the computations and results can be found in the companion paper Berkooz et al. (2021).

gist.html: With exactly marginal disorder the chaos exponent can be followed from weak coupling, where chaos may switch on only at finite coupling.

brief.html: Averaging over random couplings, as in the SYK model, makes the chaos exponent computable at large $N$; the paper does this for $N$ copies of any core theory. Normally the disorder is relevant and the exponent is found only at infinite coupling, but exactly marginal disorder keeps the theory conformal at every coupling. Then the putative exponent can be negative at weak coupling, so chaos may switch on only at a finite coupling, which the paper compares with the KAM theorem.

children.title: The SYK model at large N: self-energy and ladders
children.body: In the SYK model, $N$ Majorana fermions interact through $J_{i_1\dots i_q}\chi_{i_1}\cdots\chi_{i_q}$ with Gaussian random couplings of variance $\propto J^2/N^{q-1}$. Averaging over the couplings ties pairs of interaction vertices together, and at large $N$ only “melonic” diagrams survive. The averaged propagator $G$ then obeys a closed Schwinger–Dyson equation, $G^{-1}=G_0^{-1}-\Sigma$ with self-energy $\Sigma=J^2G^{q-1}$; this can be packaged as the saddle point of a bilocal action in $G$ and $\Sigma$, the $G$–$\Sigma$ formalism. At order $1/N$ the connected four-point function is a sum of ladder diagrams, each rung adding two vertices joined by $q-2$ propagators: $\mathcal F=\sum_nK^n\mathcal F_0$. The paper keeps this structure around a general core CFT, where the free propagator is replaced by the core CFT and its higher correlators enter the self-energy and the kernel.

gist.html: The Schwinger–Dyson equation in diagrams, and the first subtracted $n$-point functions entering it.

First, although the kernel is very complicated, knowing that an iterative ladder structure exists for the four-point function is already an important result since it allows for a systematic computation of , as we now discuss. Second, although a full solution of the two- and four-point functions requires knowing all -point functions of the core CFT, a solution to order in perturbation theory in only requires knowing the -point functions for .

gist.html: The ladder makes $\lambda_L$ systematically computable; order $J^{2n}$ needs only core correlators up to $2n+2$ points.
Two- and four-point functions obey SYK-like equations with a ladder kernel built from all core correlators.

brief.html: At leading order in $1/N$ the averaged two-point function obeys a Schwinger–Dyson equation like SYK's, except that every correlator of the core CFT enters, through theory-independent “subtracted” combinations. The connected four-point function is again a sum of ladders, $C=\sum_nK^nF_0$, now with a far more complicated kernel. Still, at order $J^{2n}$ only correlators of up to $2n+2$ points are needed, so the kernel can be computed perturbatively.

children.title: The chaos exponent as a kernel eigenvalue
children.body: If the double commutator obeys a ladder equation $(1-K_R)W_R=F_0$, its late-time behaviour is governed by the kernel alone. The source $F_0$, a single rung, does not grow, while the ladder sums an unbounded number of rungs. A late-time growing piece of $W_R$ must therefore solve the homogeneous equation $K_RW_R=W_R$: it is an eigenfunction of the retarded kernel with eigenvalue one. Because the averaged theory is conformal, one can try a function of definite growth, $\propto e^{\lambda(t_1+t_2)/2}$, which the kernel maps to itself times an eigenvalue $k_R(\lambda)$. The chaos exponent is then the largest $\lambda$ with $k_R(\lambda)=1$. This is how $\lambda_L$ was computed in SYK by Kitaev and by Maldacena and Stanford, and the paper applies it to the retarded kernel of a general disordered CFT.

If , the ladder structure (however complicated) allows us to compute it in cases where the averaged correlator has conformal symmetry (see Murugan et al. (2017) for a review). This is done by finding the largest solution of the equation , where are the eigenvalues of the retarded kernel . If then we can identify , and otherwise we learn that .

gist.html: The largest solution of $k_R(\lambda)=1$ is $\lambda_L$ if positive; otherwise there is no chaos.

If the integral diverges at a positive (negative) value of , we have a continuous (discontinuous) transition into chaos.

At arbitrarily weak coupling this behavior seems to control the behavior of the disordered theory double-commutator. The result is striking: in order to determine the type of transition into chaos, it is enough to find (the sign of) in a single core CFT. The retarded kernel gives $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$; its weak-coupling limit, conjecturally a single core CFT's $\lambda_L^0$, sets the onset.

brief.html: The double commutator obeys a retarded version of the ladder, and the largest $\lambda$ at which the retarded kernel has eigenvalue one gives the chaos exponent if it is positive, and no chaos otherwise. For exactly marginal disorder that eigenvalue is a series in $J$, whose leading term already fixes the sign of the exponent at weak coupling, and so the type of onset. The paper conjectures $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)=\lambda_L^0$, the late-time exponent of the decoupled core CFT.

gist.html: Any disordered CFT keeps SYK's ladder structure; for marginal disorder, weak coupling fixes the type of onset.

brief.html: Around any core CFT, the large-$N$ disorder average keeps the structure known from SYK: a self-consistent two-point function and a four-point function built as a ladder. The double commutator obeys a real-time version of the ladder, and the growth rate at which its kernel has eigenvalue one is the chaos exponent, when positive. For exactly marginal disorder this can be expanded in the coupling, and the leading order decides whether chaos sets in continuously. The paper conjectures that this is decided by one core CFT alone.

Generalized free fields (GFFs) are non-local theories with no energy-momentum tensor, but can be obtained by specific large-flavor limits of local theories, and are good toy-models for more complicated theories. brief.html: The 1d example, the cSYK model, couples generalized free fermions of dimension $\Delta=1/q$ by SYK-like disorder, which is exactly marginal at leading order in $1/N$. Its retarded kernel is known in closed form, and the putative exponent runs from $-2\Delta$ at weak coupling to the maximal value 1 at strong coupling. So there is no chaos below a finite coupling, a discontinuous onset. The 2d $\mathcal N=2$ version, conformal even at finite $N$, behaves the same way.

children.body:
We now discuss the disordered 2d minimal models. A single core CFT in this case consists of an SUSY minimal model, which can be represented by a single chiral superfield and superpotential . The full disordered theory is then

(19)

We emphasize that we interpret this equation in conformal perturbation theory in around copies of the minimal model, where is the chiral operator of dimension which appears in . Since the CFT at has no continuous non-R global symmetries, every classically marginal operator is exactly marginal Green et al. (2010); Kol (2002); Kol (2010), and so each deformation for is exactly marginal. Thus each realization of the model is conformal, and as a result averaged correlators of will also be conformal (even at finite ).

gist.html: Random superpotential couplings between $\mathcal N=2$ $A_{q-1}$ minimal models are exactly marginal, so every realization is conformal.

children.title: N=2 minimal models as Landau–Ginzburg theories
children.body: A two-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ theory of one chiral superfield $\Phi$ with superpotential $W=\Phi^q$ flows in the infrared to a superconformal fixed point, the $A_{q-1}$ minimal model, with central charge $c=3(q-2)/q$. A theory of chiral superfields defined by its superpotential in this way is called a Landau–Ginzburg theory. The superpotential is not renormalized and must have R-charge 2, which fixes the R-charge of $\Phi$ to $2/q$ and its scaling dimension to $1/q$. Its powers $\Phi^k$ with $k\le q-2$ form the chiral ring. A superpotential term built from $q$ chiral fields of dimension $1/q$ is classically marginal. Results of Green, Komargodski, Seiberg, Tachikawa and Wecht, and of Kol, show that, absent continuous non-R global symmetries, such terms are exactly marginal. For $q=3$, $c=1$ and the model is a free compact boson at a specific radius, so its chiral field is a vertex operator whose correlators are all known.

We can now attempt to compute in perturbation theory. This computation is generically difficult, and so we focus on the case , where a core CFT has central charge and so corresponds to the free compact boson at a specific radius. We can identify the operators in terms of vertex operators of the boson, and as a result we can read off all -point functions of the . Using this result to compute the leading contribution to the retarded kernel at small given in (10), we find that at small the exponent approaches zero. As a result, we expect a continuous transition into chaos in this model, as in figure 1a. In particular, the value of in a single minimal model is also zero, so that the conjecture (13) is again obeyed.

gist.html: At $q=3$, a $c=1$ boson per copy, $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ and $\lambda_L^0$ both vanish: a continuous onset is expected.
For the disordered $A_2$ minimal model $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}\to0$ at weak coupling, so a continuous onset is expected.

brief.html: Copies of the $\mathcal N=2$ $A_{q-1}$ minimal model coupled by random superpotential terms are conformal for every realization, because every classically marginal operator there is exactly marginal. For $q=3$ each copy is a $c=1$ compact boson, whose correlators are all known. The leading kernel then gives a putative exponent that tends to zero at weak coupling, so a continuous onset is expected.

gist.html: Disordered generalized free fields switch chaos on discontinuously, the $A_2$ minimal model continuously; both obey the conjecture.

brief.html: For disordered generalized free fields in 1d and 2d the putative exponent tends to $-2\Delta$ at weak coupling, so there is no chaos until a finite coupling: the onset is discontinuous. For the disordered $\mathcal N=2$ $A_2$ minimal model it tends to zero instead, and a continuous onset is expected. In both classes the weak-coupling limit equals the late-time exponent $\lambda_L^0$ of a single core CFT, as conjectured.

  2. 2
    We implicitly assumed that the chaos exponent increases monotonically with the strength of the disorder . As we start with N decoupled systems it is reasonable, but not necessarily true. For example, an integrable deformation keeps the exponent at zero, but these are hard to come by in this context.

gist.html:
• Context SYK-like disorder gives the chaos exponent $\lambda_L$, usually only at infinite coupling. How does chaos start?
  • Result
    • Randomly coupled copies of any CFT obey SYK-like large-$N$ equations; their ladder kernel gives a putative exponent.
    • Exactly marginal disorder keeps the theory conformal at every coupling, so $\lambda_L$ can be followed from weak to strong.
    • Disordered generalized free fields have weak-coupling putative exponent $-2\Delta<0$: a discontinuous onset, at finite coupling.
    • A disordered supersymmetric minimal model's putative exponent tends to zero at small coupling: a continuous onset is expected.
  • Why it matters The paper calls the discontinuous transition into chaos surprising, comparing it with classical KAM theory.

specialist.html:
• Context Relevant SYK-like disorder gives $\lambda_L$ only in the IR, at infinite coupling. How does chaos set in?
  • Result
    • Copies of any CFT with random $q$-body couplings obey large-$N$ Schwinger–Dyson and ladder equations; the retarded kernel $K_R$ gives $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$.
    • For exactly marginal disorder the eigenvalues of $K_R$ are series in $J^2$, each order needing finitely many core correlators.
    • With $\lambda_L=\max(0,\lambda_L^{\text{ker}})$, the sign of $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)$ sets a continuous or discontinuous onset; the paper claims $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)=\lambda_L^0$, one core CFT's late-time exponent, shown under reasonable assumptions in a companion paper.
    • Disordered generalized free fields, 1d and 2d supersymmetric, have $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}\to-2\Delta$: a discontinuous onset, and SYK values at large $J$.
    • The disordered supersymmetric $A_2$ minimal model ($c=1$ bosons) has $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}\to0$: a continuous onset is expected. Both obey the claimed equality.
  • Why it matters The paper calls the discontinuous transition into chaos surprising, comparing it with classical chaos, above all the KAM theorem.

student.html:
• Context SYK-like random couplings usually give quantum chaos's growth rate $\lambda_L$ only at infinite coupling. How does it begin?
  • Result
    • Randomly coupled copies of any conformal theory obey SYK-like equations; a ladder kernel gives a putative exponent.
    • If the coupling never runs (exactly marginal), the theory stays conformal, so $\lambda_L$ can be followed from weak to strong.
    • Disordered generalized free fields have a negative putative exponent at weak coupling: a discontinuous onset, at finite coupling.
    • A disordered supersymmetric minimal model's exponent tends to zero at small coupling: chaos should start continuously.
  • Why it matters The paper calls the discontinuous transition into chaos surprising, comparing it with classical KAM theory.

brief.html:
The chaos exponent $\lambda_L$ is the growth rate of a thermal double commutator, a quantum Lyapunov exponent. Averaging over random couplings, as in the SYK model, makes it computable at large $N$. But such disorder is usually relevant, so $\lambda_L$ is found only in the infrared, at effectively infinite coupling. The paper couples $N$ copies of a core CFT by random, exactly marginal interactions of strength $J$, and follows $\lambda_L$ from weak to strong coupling. Chaos then sets in either at once or only at a finite coupling: disordered generalized free fields show the second, a disordered minimal model the first. The paper compares the delayed onset with classical chaos, above all the KAM theorem.

At leading order in $1/N$ the averaged two-point function obeys a Schwinger–Dyson equation like SYK's, but every correlator of the core CFT enters it, through theory-independent “subtracted” combinations. The four-point function is still a sum of ladders built from one kernel. So is the double commutator, with a retarded kernel. The largest $\lambda$ at which that kernel has eigenvalue one, $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$, is the chaos exponent when positive; otherwise there is no chaos, and $\lambda_L=\max(0,\lambda_L^{\text{ker}})$.

With exactly marginal disorder every realization is conformal, and the kernel's eigenvalue is a series in $J$, each order needing finitely many core correlators. The leading order fixes $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)$, and its sign decides the onset: continuous if positive, discontinuous if negative. The paper conjectures $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)=\lambda_L^0$, the late-time exponent of the double commutator of one decoupled core CFT, never positive in unitary 2d theories. A single core CFT would then decide how chaos sets in.

In 1d the cSYK model couples generalized free fermions of dimension $\Delta=1/q$, and its kernel is known in closed form. The putative exponent rises to the maximal value 1 at strong coupling but tends to $-2\Delta$ at weak coupling. So there is no chaos below a finite coupling, and $\lambda_L^0=-2\Delta$ agrees with the conjecture. The 2d supersymmetric version, conformal even at finite $N$, behaves the same way. Copies of the supersymmetric $A_2$ minimal model, each a $c=1$ boson, are exactly marginally coupled. Their leading kernel gives an exponent tending to zero, so a continuous onset is expected, again with $\lambda_L^0$ matching.

The equality of $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)$ and $\lambda_L^0$ is conjectured, argued in a companion paper under reasonable assumptions, and checked only in these examples. For the minimal model only the leading weak-coupling kernel is computed, for $q=3$. The classification assumes $\lambda_L$ grows monotonically with $J$, which the paper calls reasonable but not guaranteed. The comparison with the KAM theorem stays a comparison: no quantum analogue of it is proved.

defs.html: The rate $\lambda_L$ at which a thermal double commutator of two operators grows in time, $\sim e^{\lambda_Lt}$: a quantum counterpart of a classical Lyapunov exponent. With temperature set by $\beta=2\pi$, as in this paper, its largest allowed value is $\lambda_L=1$, and $\lambda_L=0$ means no chaos.

The thermal expectation value of a squared commutator, $\langle[U(t),W(0)]^2\rangle_\beta$, of operators at different times. It measures how strongly an early perturbation affects a later measurement. In a chaotic large-$N$ system it starts at order $1/N$ and grows like $e^{\lambda_Lt}/N$.

The Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev model: $N$ Majorana fermions in $0+1$ dimensions with a random all-to-all $q$-body interaction, averaged over the couplings. It is solvable at large $N$, nearly conformal at low energy and maximally chaotic there. In this paper's language it is a disordered free-fermion theory, with relevant disorder.

How the chaos exponent $\lambda_L(J)$ leaves zero as the disorder $J$ is turned on, assumed to grow with $J$. Continuous: $\lambda_L$ is positive for every $J>0$. Discontinuous: $\lambda_L$ stays exactly zero up to a finite coupling and only then rises, because $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ is negative at weak coupling.

at.quote: two possible behaviors for the onset of chaos

defs.html: The Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem of classical mechanics: when an integrable Hamiltonian system is perturbed weakly enough, most of its invariant tori survive, deformed, so most motion stays regular rather than chaotic. The paper compares its own finding, no chaos below a finite disorder, with results of this kind.

The theory $\mathcal Q$ of which the paper takes $N$ decoupled copies before coupling them by disorder. It may be any quantum field theory or spin system; the paper focuses on a conformal one, and its correlation functions are the input to every computation.

Said of a deformation that leaves a CFT conformal at every value of its coupling: its beta function vanishes to all orders, so no renormalization group flow starts. An operator that is only classically marginal can become relevant or irrelevant through quantum corrections; the disorder of SYK is relevant.

Computing the correlators of a CFT deformed by a coupling times an integrated operator as a power series in the coupling, each term an integrated correlator of the undeformed CFT. The paper defines its disordered CFTs this way, as a series in $J$.

The paper's name for $N$ copies of a core CFT deformed by $\sum J_{i_1\dots i_q}\mathcal O_{i_1}\cdots\mathcal O_{i_q}$, a product of $q$ copies of a primary operator with Gaussian random couplings of variance set by $J^2$, read in conformal perturbation theory. SYK is the case of free fermions.

at.quote: We call such theories disordered CFTs

defs.html: The statement that a correlator is a sum of ladder diagrams, $C=\sum_nK^nF_0$, each rung the same operator $K$, the kernel, acting on the previous ones. In SYK the kernel is one simple rung; around a general core CFT it contains all of that CFT's correlators, but the iterative form survives.

at.quote: establish the existence of a kernel structure

defs.html: The paper's $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$: the largest $\lambda$ at which the retarded kernel has eigenvalue one. When it is positive it is the chaos exponent. When it is negative the computation's assumptions fail and the true exponent vanishes, so $\lambda_L=\max(0,\lambda_L^{\text{ker}})$.

The space of couplings of a CFT's exactly marginal deformations, each point of which is again a CFT. Here one realization of the random couplings $J_{i_1\dots i_q}$ is a point on it, and the disorder average is a non-uniform, Gaussian, average over the manifold.

Theories whose correlators are exactly those of a free field of arbitrary dimension $\Delta$: every $n$-point function is a sum of products of two-point functions. They have no stress tensor, so they are not local theories, but they arise in large-$N$ limits of local ones.

Here the $\mathcal N=2$ superconformal $A_{q-1}$ minimal model: the infrared fixed point of one chiral superfield $\Phi$ with superpotential $W=\Phi^q$, of central charge $c=3(q-2)/q$, in which $\Phi$ has dimension $1/q$. For $q=3$ it is a free compact boson at a specific radius.

An exact equation for a full propagator $G$ in terms of a self-energy $\Sigma$ built from $G$ itself. With disorder at large $N$ it closes on $G$; in SYK $\Sigma\propto J^2G^{q-1}$, while around a general core CFT $\Sigma$ also contains the CFT's higher correlators.

The kernel acting on the double commutator rather than on the ordered four-point function: the same diagrams, with the core correlators continued to real time and the new points integrated over the past light-cone. A late-time growth $e^{\lambda t}$ requires an eigenvalue $k_R(\lambda)=1$.

The model of Gross and Rosenhaus: $N$ generalized free Majorana fermions of dimension $\Delta$ in $0+1$ dimensions, coupled by the random $q$-body interaction of SYK. At $\Delta=1/q$ the coupling is classically marginal, and it is argued to be exactly marginal at leading order in $1/N$.

The paper's $\lambda_L^0$: the exponent of the late-time growth or decay of the double commutator at $J=0$, where the copies are decoupled. It is a property of one core CFT but not a chaos exponent, and is never positive in unitary 2d theories. Conjecturally it equals $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)$.

questions.q: What are $\lambda_L$, $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ and $\lambda_L^0$, and in what units?
questions.a: $\lambda_L$ is the true chaos exponent, the growth rate of the double commutator. $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ is read from the retarded kernel, the largest $\lambda$ with $k_R(\lambda)=1$; it equals $\lambda_L$ when positive, and otherwise $\lambda_L=0$. $\lambda_L^0$ is the late-time exponent of the double commutator at $J=0$, a property of one core CFT. The examples set $\beta=2\pi$, so the maximal chaos exponent is 1.

questions.q: Why does a negative $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ mean no chaos, rather than a decaying commutator?
questions.a: The kernel method looks for a growing mode of the double commutator at late times. If the largest solution of $k_R(\lambda)=1$ is negative there is no such mode, and the paper reads this as a breakdown of the approximations involved, not as a negative exponent. The true chaos exponent then simply vanishes, which gives $\lambda_L=\max(0,\lambda_L^{\text{ker}})$.

questions.q: In what sense is the transition into chaos discontinuous?
questions.a: In the discontinuous case $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ is negative at small $J$, so $\lambda_L$ is exactly zero up to the finite coupling where $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}$ crosses zero, and only then rises. In the continuous case it is positive for every $J>0$. The classification assumes that the exponent grows monotonically with $J$, which the paper calls reasonable but not necessarily true.

questions.q: Why insist on exactly marginal disorder?
questions.a: Usual SYK-like disorder is relevant: the theory flows, and the kernel can be diagonalised only at the infrared fixed point, at effectively infinite coupling. If the disorder is exactly marginal, every realization of the couplings is conformal, the average is over a conformal manifold, and the kernel's eigenvalue can be expanded order by order in $J$. Only then can one see how chaos starts at weak coupling.

questions.q: Why should a single, undeformed core CFT decide how chaos sets in?
questions.a: At weak coupling the leading term of $k_R(\lambda)$ is an integral of a core CFT commutator, and $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)$ is the largest $\lambda$ at which it diverges. The divergence comes from large negative times, where the core CFT's double commutator behaves as $e^{\lambda_L^0t}$. So, under reasonable assumptions argued in a companion paper, the two agree, and the paper conjectures this in general.

questions.q: What happens at strong disorder in the examples?
questions.a: For the 1d cSYK model the putative exponent approaches the maximal value $\lambda_L=1$ at large $J$, as in the SYK model, for any $\Delta$. For the 2d $\mathcal N=2$ generalized free fields it approaches the value of the 2d supersymmetric versions of SYK. Between weak and strong coupling both curves are computed exactly, which is what exact marginality buys.

questions.q: How far does the comparison with the KAM theorem go?
questions.a: The paper calls it tempting: in both, weak perturbations leave a system without chaos, which appears only beyond a finite strength. To sharpen the comparison it asks what a single core CFT must obey for the onset to be discontinuous, and answers through the conjecture, $\lambda_L^0<0$. It does not formulate or prove a quantum analogue of the theorem.

questions.q: What does the paper not show?
questions.a: The equality $\lambda_L^{\text{ker}}(0^+)=\lambda_L^0$ is a conjecture, argued in a companion paper under reasonable assumptions and checked in the two examples. For the minimal model only the leading weak-coupling kernel is computed, for $q=3$, so the continuous onset is expected rather than followed to strong coupling. The classification assumes $\lambda_L$ grows monotonically with $J$.
